blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the emerging concept of 'far memory'—memory attached to the network that can be remotely accessed without CPU mediation—as a compelling future choice for data center applications due to its potential for higher capacity, separate scaling, better availability, and shareability. However, he notes the trade-off between fast one-sided access (without remote CPU involvement) and traditional RPC-style access, emphasizing the need for new data structures designed specifically for far memory. The paper argues that most existing data structures are ill-suited for far memory due to their reliance on multiple remote accesses, and proposes hardware extensions (indirect addressing, scatter-gather, and notifications) to enable efficient far-memory data structures. The authors demonstrate how these extensions can be used to design efficient counters, maps (HT-tree), queues, and refreshable vectors, with a case study of a monitoring application.
paper_title: Designing Far Memory Data Structures: Think Outside the Box
paper_abstract: Technologies like RDMA and Gen-Z, which give access to memory outside the box, are gaining in popularity. These technologies provide the abstraction of far memory, where memory is attached to the network and can be accessed by remote processors without mediation by a local processor. Unfortunately, far memory is hard to use because existing data structures are mismatched to it. We argue that we need new data structures for far memory, borrowing techniques from concurrent data structures and distributed systems. We examine the requirements of these data structures and show how to realize them using simple hardware extensions. ACM Reference Format: Marcos K. Aguilera, Kimberly Keeton, Stanko Novakovic, and Sharad Singhal. 2019. Designing Far Memory Data Structures: Think Outside the Box. In Workshop on Hot Topics in Operating Systems (HotOS ’19), May 13–15, 2019, Bertinoro, Italy. ACM, New York, NY, USA, 7 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3317550.3321433
